name: Rhinofire
whyHere: You put down the blade, or you were sent away from it, or you are looking for a line worth holding that isn't theirs.

inventory.name: Traveler's Pack
inventory.description: A worn canvas pack with good straps — bedroll, flint, mess kit, fifty small comforts of the road.

inventory.name: Waterskin
inventory.description: Boiled and refilled at the last clean spring. Worth more every week the river runs gray.

chronicle: At the Marchward trestle, Rhinofire drew the shape of what lies north from two reluctant sources: a duelist's field account of a hand going black and a listening face, and an exile's admission that the upstream structure is a pre-Transition authentication site holding the Council's backup purification sequence — gone silent eight months ago, and perhaps listening still. One final question — what should I not let it hear? — found the edge of what Eredan will carry. He refused it, finally, and returned to his barley.

turns.player: Ask the hostel-keeper if anyone else has come through from the northeast trail recently — one more voice before you commit the direction.
turns.summary: The hostel-keeper describes a lone traveler from the Disputed Zone cutoff, asking after the north road; he left a sealed, unmarked note behind.
turns.narration:
The hostel-keeper is a broad woman with flour on her apron and the unhurried manner of someone who has heard every kind of question and stopped being surprised by any of them. She's wiping down the counter when you put the question to her — anyone through from the northeast trail lately, before the melt turned the ground soft?

She thinks for a moment, setting the cloth down. "Two, maybe three days back. A man alone, coming down from the Disputed Zone cutoff. Kept his hood up, which people do, so I didn't press. But he paid in valley coin and he asked about the road north — not the way to the Redline, the *other* north, the one that goes into the Zone proper." She picks the cloth back up. "He ate, he slept, he was gone before I came down in the morning. Left the bed neat, which I appreciated."

Marrow shifts on the rafter above the counter — you didn't see it get up there, but here it is, watching the keeper with the specific calm attention it reserves for things that are concluding. The keeper glances up at it, unsurprised in the way border-town people learn not to be surprised by anything, and goes back to wiping.

"He left something, actually. Forgot it or didn't want it." She reaches under the counter and sets down a small square of folded paper, sealed with a plain wax thumb-press. No mark, no name. "If you're going that direction anyway."

turns.player: Take the note and break the seal — read what was left.
turns.summary: Rhinofire breaks the seal on the unmarked note: a warning about the authentication site — it is waiting, not broken — and a single line about the wrong stag north of the second ford.
turns.narration:
The hostel-keeper slides the note across the counter without being asked — she's been waiting to be rid of it. The wax breaks clean under your thumb, plain, no sigil. Just a thumb.

Inside: six lines in a cramped, careful hand. The authentication site is not broken — it is waiting. Do not speak your name to it. Do not let it hear the water's composition — it will try to complete the protocol. If you are going anyway: the sequence it wants is the one the Council burned. It cannot be given. Tell it nothing and leave. The man who sent the survey crew back was not afraid. He was satisfied. Below that, a single line with no context: The wrong stag walks the treeline north of the second ford. Go around. No signature. The hand is educated — letters shaped with discipline — and the note smells faintly of something mineral, cold. Like stone after rain.

Marrow drops from the rafter onto the counter between you and the keeper, which she accepts with the equanimity of someone who has dealt with worse. The bird looks at the note. Then at you. Then at the treeline through the small east window, as if it already knows exactly which ford the second one is.

turns.player: Show the note to Eredan — he named the structure; he may recognize the hand or the warning's source.
turns.summary: Eredan reads the note without touching it, confirms the warning is accurate, and reveals that whoever wrote it has been north of the second ford — and recently.
turns.narration:
You cross the room and set the note on the table beside Eredan's bowl without a word. Just the paper, open, where he can read it.

He doesn't look up at first. Finishes chewing, puts his spoon down, then glances at it the way you'd glance at something you already know is going to cost you. His eyes move across the six lines slowly — too slowly for a man reading; the pace of someone making sure they haven't missed a word they hoped wasn't there.

When he's done he sits back. Doesn't touch the note.

"I don't know the hand," he says, and there's enough flatness in it that you believe him. "But the warning's right. Everything in it is right." He's quiet for a moment. "The wrong stag. That's not something people write down. That's something you only know if you've been north of the second ford." He looks up at you then — the first time he's met your eyes since his refusal. "Whoever wrote this has been there. Recently."

He pushes the note back toward you. Not away from him — toward you, specifically. His hands have stopped shaking for the first time since you sat down. "They're right about the sequence," he adds, quieter. "The Council burned it. There's no version of giving it to the structure that ends well. You go there, you say nothing. You let it run its authentication, it waits for what won't come, and eventually it stops waiting." A pause. "That's the theory. No one's stayed long enough to find out if it works."

turns.player: Pick up the note, thank Eredan, and let him return to his breakfast — you have what you came for; the road north is the next thing
turns.summary: Rhinofire took the note and thanked Eredan — the morning's two reluctant informants have given what they'll give. The road north is next.
turns.narration:
You pick up the note and fold it once along the crease it already holds, then tuck it inside your coat. The mineral smell comes with it — cold stone and something else, faint, like water that has sat in the dark a long time.

"Thank you," you say to Eredan, and you mean it plainly. No ceremony. He nods once — the nod of a man who has said his piece and is glad to stop saying it. His hand finds the spoon again and he turns to the barley without looking back up at you.

The hostel-keeper is already looking elsewhere, the cloth moving in slow circles on the counter. Marrow shifts on her counter-edge, settles, and watches you cross toward the door with that particular stillness it holds when something is about to begin.

The morning outside is early-spring cold — the melt has made the ground soft and the air smells of wet earth and yesterday's frost. The road north from the Marchward starts just past the waygate's neutral ground: an unpaved track that turns to mud a hundred paces in and keeps going. According to the note, the second ford is where the wrong stag walks the treeline. You haven't been there yet. The structure is beyond it.

turns.player: Read the fight ahead — stand in the doorway and let your sense of what comes next settle before you move
turns.summary: Rhinofire stands in the hostel doorway and reads the road north — the wrong stag territorial and real past the second ford, the authentication structure a held breath rather than a threat, the danger there a matter of words rather than force.
turns.narration:
You stop in the doorway — not hesitating, just standing. The morning light comes in flat and grey through the hostel's small windows, and you let the shape of the day ahead settle into you the way your training said it would: not thought, exactly, but attention finding its own level.

The Marchward is waking outside. You can hear the specific sounds of a border town in early spring: boot mud on a wooden step, a trader haggling in a language that isn't quite valley-common, the drip of snowmelt from the hostel eaves. None of it is urgent. The road north will be mud past the first fork and worse past the second — you already knew that. What the read gives you is the texture of what waits there.

The wrong stag is real. You feel it the way you feel a line before it snaps — not a fact you've assembled but a certainty that arrives whole. North of the second ford, in the treeline, something that used to die has stopped being willing to. It is not aggressive by nature. It is territorial by something older than aggression: the sense that it belongs to a crossing and the crossing belongs to it. You will not take it by surprise. You will not go around it without it knowing. What you can choose is the ground — and when you meet it, whether you stand or run first.

The authentication structure is further, and its read is quieter: a held breath, not a threat. It is waiting with the patience of something that does not experience time the way you do. The danger there is not violence. It is a question asked in the wrong language, at the wrong moment, with the wrong answer in your mouth. The note in your coat is the best map you have of what not to say. Marrow drops from the counter-edge to the floor with a soft double-tap of feet, and looks up at you once — patient, unhurried, already pointed toward the door.

turns.player: Ask someone in the Marchward about the second ford before you go — a local read on the current state of the road and what's been seen near the treeline
turns.summary: A local with muddy boots confirmed the second ford is running high on snowmelt — cross early or take the log crossing east — and reported something moving silent along the treeline at dusk, tracing the ford.
turns.narration:
You don't move from the doorway yet. The Marchward is small enough that someone local is usually within earshot, and sure enough there's a man on the step of the building opposite — thick-coated, mud on his boots to the shin, a bucket of something he's not in any hurry to carry further. He looks like he walked the north road this morning or yesterday at the latest.

You ask him about the second ford. He sets the bucket down and gives you the patient look of a man who has answered this question before.

"Ford's up," he says. "Snowmelt. You'll want to cross early if you're going — afternoon and the current's wrong. There's a log crossing a half-mile east that's still holding, if you'd rather keep your boots dry." He pauses, and something shifts in his expression — not worry, exactly, but the particular attention of someone who has noticed something he doesn't have a word for yet. "Treeline north of the ford. Something's been moving in it at dusk the last few nights. Not wolves — wolves you hear. This is quiet. Just…movement. In and out of the line, north to south, like it's tracing the crossing."

He picks the bucket back up and shrugs the way people shrug when they want to communicate that a thing has been noted and set aside and they intend to keep doing exactly that. "Probably nothing. Could be deer. But it's not deer." He nods once and goes inside.

turns.player: Read the fight — stand here a moment and let your sense of the treeline's pattern settle before you pick a route
turns.summary: Rhinofire reads the road north from the doorway — the ford clear, but the treeline pattern ambiguous: the wrong stag and the note's author may not be separate problems.
turns.narration:
You stay in the doorway another minute, letting the morning settle into you properly this time — not the hostel's warmth at your back, but the street ahead and what it connects to. The sense comes up the way it does: not vision, something more like weight. The road north. The ford. The treeline.

The ford you already understood. The log crossing east is a fact, not a read — cross early, keep to the east option if the current looks wrong. That much is clear. What the read gives you past the ford is harder to hold: there is something in the pattern up there that isn't resolved. The wrong stag, the local said. Something moving the treeline north to south at dusk, tracing the crossing. Your training wants to call it territorial — the stag holds its ground and the movement at the treeline is its circuit. But the note's author has been north of the second ford recently, and they came back with a warning about words, not teeth. Those two things don't quite sit together. Either the stag is what the local clocked and the author is a separate problem, or the movement is something the author already knows about and didn't name.

You can't press the read further from here. The second ford is where the ground speaks plainly — past it, and you'll have something true to work with.

Marrow shifts on the step beside you, cocks its head, and regards the north road with that particular sideways attention it gives to things that are heading toward a conclusion. It doesn't croak. Its silence is, as usual, timed.

turns.player: Ask Marrow plainly — is the thing in the treeline ending something, or waiting on something to end?
turns.summary: Rhinofire asked Marrow about the treeline's watcher — the bird's answer was plain: not ending, but waiting on something to end.
turns.narration:
You turn to Marrow on the step beside you and ask it plainly, the way you've learned works best: not a request, just a question put into the air where it can land.

"Is the thing in the treeline ending something, or waiting on something to end?"

Marrow shifts on the step. One foot, then the other. It looks north — not at the road, at something past the road, past the first fork and the mud and the high water of the second ford. Then it looks back at you with that eye that has seen more deaths than anything you've ever stood beside, and it is calm the way it always is, which is to say completely.

A single croak. Then, after a pause that feels timed: one more.

You've been with Marrow long enough to read the difference. The first croak is *not ending*. The second croak — the pause, then the one that follows — is *waiting*.

Waiting on something to end. Not the stag's prey. Not the note's author. Something else, something that isn't there yet. The thing in the treeline is patient in the way Marrow is patient, which tells you it is not hunting. It is attending. The distinction matters. A thing that hunts you can be turned; a thing that is waiting for you to finish something is a different problem entirely, because you have to know what you're supposed to finish first.

what-wakes-beneath.label: What Wakes Beneath
facts: [d1] Two separate clusters of people at the Marchward used the word 'substrate' unprompted — a mason's apprentice and a Marcher trader who then looked at his hand as if he'd felt something. The flickering has reached even the border-town.

[d1] The burned hand of the retreating surveyor and the exile's phrase 'no longer answers them' sit beside the substrate-talk — whatever is happening in the upper structure may be the same stirring felt in people's hands at the Marchward.

[d1] The surveyor's listening face — hearing something no one else could, hand pressed to his chest as the blackness spread — reads less like a wound and more like a signal received. Something at the upstream structure may be transmitting, not merely malfunctioning.

[d1] Eredan's warning — 'be careful what you let it hear' — implies the authentication site may be listening. An eight-month silence followed by renewed activity suggests it did not stop; it may have been waiting for something.

[d1] The note's author states the man who sent the survey crew back was not afraid — he was satisfied. This reframes the blackened hand and the listening face: not a retreat from danger but a completion of something. Someone may have intended what happened to the surveyor.
[d1] The authentication structure reads as a held breath — not threatening, but waiting with a patience outside human time. The danger there is a question asked wrong, not a force to be withstood.

facts: [d1] Mercenary contractor, recently through the Disputed Zone
[d1] Her relief after speaking is professional — information given, weight transferred. She is watching the exile the way she'd watch a potential threat: assessing, not hostile.

stillhold-exile-marchward.label: Stillhold exile
facts: [d1] Former Stillhold resident, now sheltering at the Marchward
[d1] His posture after confessing reads as guilt, not relief — he feels personally implicated in the Council losing contact with the upstream structure, not merely informed about it.
[d1] When asked directly about the upstream structure, he drew a line: 'I've said what I can say' — distinguishing what he knows from what he will speak. The limit is deliberate, not ignorance.

[d1] Named himself Eredan — no surname offered. Confirmed the structure's nature and gave a final warning: be careful what you let it hear. Carries the weight of knowing personally, not institutionally.

[d1] Asked to accompany the journey north; refused flatly and finally — a single word, no explanation. Drew back into silence and began eating. The refusal reads as decided long before the question was asked.

marchward-note-author.label: The Note's Author
facts: [d1] The note is written in an educated, disciplined hand — smells of cold stone and mineral water. No name, no mark. Left two to three days before Rhinofire arrived. Knew the structure's nature, knew the burned sequence, and knew the name of a specific beast north of the second ford: the wrong stag.
[d1] Eredan confirmed: whoever wrote the note has been north of the second ford, and recently — the wrong stag is not something people write down without firsthand knowledge.

[d1] The wrong stag is territorial, not aggressive by instinct — it holds a crossing the way something older than violence holds ground. Meeting it is a matter of choosing the ground and the moment, not avoiding it entirely.

[d1] Something has been moving silent in the treeline north of the second ford at dusk — north-south, tracing the crossing — for at least the last few nights. A local ruled out wolves and deer. This predates Rhinofire's arrival and may relate to the wrong stag or to whoever wrote the note.

[d1] The wrong stag and the treeline movement may not be separate problems — the author went north of the second ford and returned with a warning about words; the pattern at the treeline doesn't resolve cleanly into 'stag holds ground' alone. The distinction between the two is something only the ground…

[d1] Marrow's read: the thing in the treeline is not hunting — it is waiting on something to end. It attends rather than pursues. This changes the threat shape: not predator behavior, but witness behavior. Whatever it waits on, the ending has not yet arrived.

personalArc.name: The Weight of the Net
personalArc.premise: A fisher from the edge of the world who put down the blade — or was put down by it — carries the Marchward in their hands and a village in their chest, and must decide whether righting wrongs means picking the blade back up, or finding something the blade was never built to fix.
personalArc.stakes: To hold the line they chose when they walked away, or discover that walking away was itself the wound they have been circling — and that the village they came from is the thing the world will eventually ask them to pay with.

chronicleCache.hash: d0|b|c|q|L1|To right the wrongs of the world
chronicleCache.text: You have become someone who carries a grievance older than your own name — a fury at wrongs not yet righted, a moral weight that sits in the chest like a coal still finding its heat. The Marchers know your face now, have registered your presence among them the way a wall registers a first crack: noted, not yet tested. The Ashwardens and the Unmakers have heard nothing particular about you, which means the world still holds its breath. Even the Stillhold watches from a wary distance, as if they sense something in you that hasn't declared itself yet. You have done nothing of consequence — not yet. That is the whole of the pressure.
